texts.orig: If you’re a product manager or builder shipping AI features or products, you’ve probably felt this:
texts.text: If you’re a product manager or builder shipping AI features or products, you’ve probably felt this:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Your company is under pressure to launch something with AI. A promising idea takes shape. The team nails the demo, the early reviews look good, and stakeholders are excited. You push hard to ship it to production.
texts.text: Your company is under pressure to launch something with AI. A promising idea takes shape. The team nails the demo, the early reviews look good, and stakeholders are excited. You push hard to ship it to production.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Then things start to break. You’re deep in the weeds, trying to figure out what went wrong. But the issues are tangled and hard to trace, and nothing points to a single fix. Suddenly your entire product approach feels shaky.
texts.text: Then things start to break. You’re deep in the weeds, trying to figure out what went wrong. But the issues are tangled and hard to trace, and nothing points to a single fix. Suddenly your entire product approach feels shaky.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We’ve seen this play out again and again. Over the past few years, we’ve helped over 50 companies design, ship, and scale AI-powered autonomous systems with thousands of customers.
texts.text: We’ve seen this play out again and again. Over the past few years, we’ve helped over 50 companies design, ship, and scale AI-powered autonomous systems with thousands of customers.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Across all of these experiences, we’ve seen a common pitfall: people overlook the fact that AI systems fundamentally break the assumptions of traditional software products.

texts.orig: When companies don’t recognize these differences, their AI products face ripple effects like unexpected failures and poor decision-making. We’ve seen so many teams experience the painful shift from an impressive demo to a system that can’t scale or sustain. And along the way, user trust in the product quietly erodes.
texts.text: When companies don’t recognize these differences, their AI products face ripple effects like unexpected failures and poor decision-making. We’ve seen so many teams experience the painful shift from an impressive demo to a system that can’t scale or sustain. And along the way, user trust in the product quietly erodes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: After seeing this pattern play out many times, we developed a new framework for the AI product development lifecycle, based on what we’ve seen in successful deployments. It’s designed to recognize the uniqueness of AI systems and help you build more intentional, stable, and trustworthy products. By the end of this post, you should be able to map your own product to this framework and have a better sense of how to start, where to focus, and how to scale safely.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Let’s walk through the ways that building AI products is different from traditional software.
texts.text: Let’s walk through the ways that building AI products is different from traditional software.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 1. AI products are inherently non-deterministic
texts.text: 1. AI products are inherently non-deterministic

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Traditional software behaves more or less predictably. Users interact in known ways: clicking buttons, submitting forms, triggering API calls. You write logic that maps those inputs to outcomes. If something breaks, it’s usually a code issue, and you can trace it back.
texts.text: Traditional software behaves more or less predictably. Users interact in known ways: clicking buttons, submitting forms, triggering API calls. You write logic that maps those inputs to outcomes. If something breaks, it’s usually a code issue, and you can trace it back.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: AI systems behave differently.
texts.text: AI systems behave differently.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: They introduce non-determinism on both ends: in other words, there’s unpredictability in how users engage and how the system responds.
texts.text: They introduce non-determinism on both ends: in other words, there’s unpredictability in how users engage and how the system responds.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: First, the user interaction surface is far less deterministic. Instead of structured triggers like button clicks, users interact through open-ended prompts, voice commands, or other natural inputs. These are harder to validate, easier to misinterpret, and vary widely in how users express intent.
texts.text: First, the user interaction surface is far less deterministic. Instead of structured triggers like button clicks, users interact through open-ended prompts, voice commands, or other natural inputs. These are harder to validate, easier to misinterpret, and vary widely in how users express intent.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Second, the system’s behavior is inherently non-deterministic. AI models are trained to generate plausible responses based on patterns, not to follow fixed rules. The same request can produce different results depending on phrasing, context, or even a different model.
texts.text: Second, the system’s behavior is inherently non-deterministic. AI models are trained to generate plausible responses based on patterns, not to follow fixed rules. The same request can produce different results depending on phrasing, context, or even a different model.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This fundamentally changes how you build and ship. You’re no longer designing for a predictable user flow. You’re designing for

texts.label: text

texts.orig: Unlike traditional tools, AI systems are built to act with varying levels of autonomy. But here’s the part people often overlook:
texts.text: Unlike traditional tools, AI systems are built to act with varying levels of autonomy. But here’s the part people often overlook:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Every time you give an AI system more agency, you give up some control.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: at play. And that tradeoff matters (a lot!). If your system suggests a response, you can still override it. If it sends the response automatically, you’d better be sure it’s right.
texts.text: at play. And that tradeoff matters (a lot!). If your system suggests a response, you can still override it. If it sends the response automatically, you’d better be sure it’s right.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The mistake most teams make is jumping to full agency before they’ve tested what happens when the system gets it wrong. If you haven’t tested how the system behaves under high control, you’re not ready to give it high agency. And if you hand over too much agency without the system earning it first, you may lose visibility into the system, and the trust of your users.
texts.text: The mistake most teams make is jumping to full agency before they’ve tested what happens when the system gets it wrong. If you haven’t tested how the system behaves under high control, you’re not ready to give it high agency. And if you hand over too much agency without the system earning it first, you may lose visibility into the system, and the trust of your users.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: What’s more, you’re stuck debugging a large, complicated system that has taken actions you can’t trace, for reasons you’ve lost insight into, so you don’t even know what to change.

texts.orig: Evals are scoring mechanisms that help you assess whether your AI system is working, where it’s falling short, and what needs improvement. But unlike typical unit or integration tests, where inputs and outputs are fixed and correctness is binary, AI evals deal with ambiguity.

texts.orig: Where to go from here
texts.text: Where to go from here

texts.label: text
texts.orig: AI systems have the incredible potential to operate with some level of agency, but getting there is rarely about stacking complex tools or scaling things with brute force. It’s not about writing the perfect prompt either. Creating an AI system that saves time, money, and energy through effective automation is about solving the actual problem, step by step, by understanding its nuances.
texts.text: AI systems have the incredible potential to operate with some level of agency, but getting there is rarely about stacking complex tools or scaling things with brute force. It’s not about writing the perfect prompt either. Creating an AI system that saves time, money, and energy through effective automation is about solving the actual problem, step by step, by understanding its nuances.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: We often compare working with AI to onboarding a new teammate. The teammate might be brilliant, but they don’t yet know how your team works. You don’t hand them your highest-stakes projects on day one. You start small, observe, build trust, and, as they show what they can handle, you gradually expand their scope. AI systems need that same path. That’s what the CC/CD framework is designed to support.

You don’t hand them your highest-stakes projects on day one. You start small, observe, build trust, and, as they show what they can handle, you gradually expand their scope. AI systems need that same path. That’s what the CC/CD framework is designed to support.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: At the heart of CC/CD is judgment: the kind that helps you decide what to ship, how to protect users when things go wrong, when to hand control back, and how to define what “good enough” looks like.
texts.text: At the heart of CC/CD is judgment: the kind that helps you decide what to ship, how to protect users when things go wrong, when to hand control back, and how to define what “good enough” looks like.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: There’s no one-size-fits-all for how much capability to give each version, how long to gather data before moving forward, or how tightly to scope. It depends on your product, your users, and your timelines. Some products need weeks of iteration. Others can move faster. That’s where your judgment comes in.
